blocks.x: We are privileged to meet Mr. Roy Armstrong, the internationally known New Orleans jazz trumpeter and band leader. In this second program, Mr. Armstrong and his guest students from the University of Pittsburgh, Fernando Escribins from Caracas, Venezuela, Verdeet Valerius Olsen from Stockholm, Sweden, Stefan Villas-Scher from Coutre, Belgium. We'll discuss Mr. Armstrong's role as an ambassador of goodwill through his travels around the world.

When you were in Stockholm, Sweden, I know you draw tremendous crowds. And although I didn't get to see you the last time you were in Stockholm, I know that the audience never lets you leave the stage and repeat all the time. That's right.

One of our biggest successes in Stockholm, you know what I mean? I remember the first time we went there, I was booked in there by a new serial by the name of Mr. Edwald and Mr. Scarrick from Copenhagen, Denmark. They gave me three concerts at night. Our band, Mary Alice and the Gypsy Girls. And all the houses sold out. And after the concert, they had to go in the dining room of my hotel, which is a beautiful hotel that runs all over Europe because my wife traveled with me and everything. And we'd sit down there and have a wonderful time. And I'll never forget that. And then the first time in Sweden, there were so many people at the station. They gave me a trumpet of flowers and the so many things, the flowers crumbled up and I had to make a beeline back to the train. And they were wonderful. And there were people in Stockholm there and one of the sun see them or two. I remember those newspapers, Man by Page, you two cats, you know. He got a, he asked me a funny question or a question. He said, uh, there's something strong. He said, what do you think of our beautiful Swedish girls? You know. I said, well I tell you, my wife travels with me. She travels with me all the time. And she's got the best smorgasbord in the world. And I'll never forget all Sweden. We played in the cottage party. And that's that concert over there, that beautiful piano, that sound. And during intermission, we were standing outside with our collars up, you know, kind of, people get cold. And there was three of his boys come up to Jack Tay Garden and he says, you photo for me. And Jack said, well I tell you, I live two blocks from the concert hall. He said, yeah. He said, yeah. He said, yeah. He said, now, if I go there, I'll catch cold, you know. He said, yeah. He said, yeah. He said, you wouldn't want me to catch cold. He said, yeah. And he remember Alice Babs. Oh yeah. Well, that's the girl that got our inspiration the first night she sang with us in Stockholm. She sang about three or four numbers in this world of the house. And now she's in America doing wonderful. And we're talking about those moments. I've been talking about Sweden, you know. I'm done.
Do you think European people over there have just feeling they're good, though? Anyway, you're worried about it.

The audience is going to enjoy you and things. The people there come there to hear what we're going to do. And from the moment we hit pale moon shining, you know the theme song, everybody sits right there and relax. And from that first note on, the warmth is there. Yeah. Right there in your country, Belgium. A dear friend of mine, Robert Guffin, he's a big lawyer there. And he wrote a book on frontier of jazz years ago. Where we were born probably, you know. That's how far back Belgium is enjoying good jazz and good music.
I think they have, but do you feel the same way?

He was so deep in that music. The same as I am. So during the Second World War, when he had to come to America to meet our president, to Washington, D.C. He got off the plane in New York. And I was playing at the Paramount Theater. And before he moved to play for Washington, he came and spent two days with Satsang. Backstage, sort of out there, playing tapes. See, now I go to Washington. That's like we're pretty big in California. See? And then, when we went into your country, Caracas, I have an album right now that they presented me, a beautiful album, like a scrapbook. And I kept it home until I got sick and split to Italy. And I received so many telegrams with a nice them all on the wall. And when I got home, she took them down, you know, to go home. Now I'm putting those telegrams in that little album, you know, like that big, beautiful thing. Every telegram that was given to me, and I covered up with sketch tape, the most beautiful thing ever seen.
Do you think your audience in Caracas was as responsive to jazz, or to American jazz, as those audiences in Europe and in the United States? Everywhere in the world. Everywhere.

It's the same. Notes and notes in any language. Now, let me tell you a thing. At the time we was there, they was having that little scrimmage. The president, what, blah, blah, you know what's happening. And they were supposed to bomb the university where we played that night. Yeah. And there wasn't a student thinking about it. Sure. Then nothing happened. We played for the president's party. Nothing happened. And we played after that in a hotel downtown, Pack House. And then we played in the bullring, concerts night. And Trummy and I, we handled up Tiger Rags and the people who had a role and he, they gave us a wooden sword. And, uh, to give Trummy a horn and the kids. Good laughs and, you know, headaches and, you know, there's so many people who were separated and they meet at the concert and go back together and things like that. That's what music supposed to do. Any time you don't appreciate music to that extent, but you have to feel good to do that. Take care of your health and things like that. And we look forward to every night we play. segments.title: Program introduction and question about Stockholm crowds
segments.summary: The announcer introduces Armstrong and three visiting students and the topic of his goodwill travels; a student raises Stockholm audiences.

segments.title: First Swedish tour: concerts, flowers, and Alice Babs
segments.summary: Armstrong recalls his first Stockholm concerts, the crowds at the station, a reporter's question about Swedish girls, Jack Teagarden at the concert hall, and Alice Babs singing with the band.

segments.title: European audiences, Belgian friend Robert Goffin, and Caracas telegram album
segments.summary: Armstrong says audiences warm to the theme song, mentions his Belgian lawyer friend who wrote on jazz and visited him backstage during the war, and describes the scrapbook of telegrams from Caracas.

segments.title: Playing Caracas: unrest, the bullring act with Trummy, and his tape collection
segments.summary: Music is the same in any language; Armstrong tells of playing Caracas during political unrest, the bullfight comedy bit with Trummy Young, and indexing his souvenir tapes.

segments.chapter: New Orleans lineage and brass bands
segments.title: Who owns the music: generations of New Orleans players and brass bands
segments.summary: Asked about American versus German jazz, Armstrong says no one can say who copied whom, traces the lineage Merritt, Buddy Bolden, Oliver, and recalls brass band parades and second liners.

segments.title: Playing Caracas television with a local band
segments.summary: Armstrong describes a TV show in Caracas with two bands, an opera overture in jazz, and his theme song.

segments.title: Improvising on Latin and foreign music; cool jazz-style attitudes and humor
segments.summary: Armstrong says any music can be improvised if played with good feeling, praises Eddie Calvert, praises clown bands, and says European audiences take popular songs as seriously as any.

segments.title: Feeling at home with audiences around the world
segments.summary: A student asks how it feels to draw audiences everywhere; Armstrong says he thinks of himself as a neighborhood boy and first went to Sweden in 1934.

segments.chapter: Growing up and learning in New Orleans
segments.title: Childhood New Orleans: honky-tonks, blues, and Oliver's funeral band
segments.summary: Asked about dreams as a kid, Armstrong describes the Storyville honky-tonks and tells of Joe Oliver's brass band breaking up a ball game on the way back from a funeral.

segments.chapter: Growing up and learning in New Orleans
segments.title: Funeral marches today and opinion on cool jazz
segments.summary: Brass bands still play funerals; Armstrong then says cool jazz reminds him of a lazy trumpet player and he prefers players who go for the high note.

segments.chapter: Growing up and learning in New Orleans
segments.title: Early New Orleans playing by ear, practice, travel, and the Waifs' Home band
segments.summary: Armstrong explains how early bands had one reader and the rest played by ear, talks about warming up and touring with his wife, and recalls learning cornet at thirteen in the Waifs' Home band and the handkerchief habit of players.

segments.title: Handkerchiefs in Caracas and missing the bullfight
segments.summary: A light exchange about needing a handkerchief in Caracas and the promoter's joke that Armstrong could be a bullfighter.

segments.title: Why music appeals the same in Sweden, Jerusalem, and Africa
segments.summary: Asked why he appeals everywhere, Armstrong says records carry the feeling, mentions Bert Williams records, and recalls audiences in Jerusalem and Africa.

segments.title: Closing remarks and preview of part three
segments.summary: A student shares an anecdote about a convert to jazz and the announcer closes the program and previews the next.
